newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FORECAST-Jardine Fleming sees Pakistan stocks up.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Jardine Fleming sees Pakistan stocks up.

text.p: Pakistan's depressed stock markets could surge after parliamentary elections scheduled for February 3, a leading analyst said on Tuesday.

John Style, country head of Jardine Fleming Pakistan (Private) Ltd, told Reuters in an interview that better times could be ahead for the Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index, which stood at 1,429 points at midsession on Tuesday.
"Post-election, we could see a rally that would move the KSE trading band up by 100 to 150 points," he said.
"There can be no doubt that Pakistan is facing major economic and political problems. However, we believe these problems will eventually be resolved," he added.
President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
He appointed a caretaker government led by Prime Minister Meraj Khalid to supervise national and provincial polls, launch a drive against corruption and initiate economic reforms.
Style said political uncertainty before the elections would keep the index in a narrow band, but that the market had already discounted most of the negative possibilities.
He listed several factors that could spark an upturn.

"Resumption of the IMF support programme, elections, an easing in domestic liquidity, performance in emerging markets generally and South Asia particularly, and finally, the future direction of U.S. interest rates could potentially trigger a bull run," he said.

Style said Jardine Fleming had cut its earnings forecast for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) to 14 percent due to the freezing of corporate tax rates at 36 percent and the central bank's tight monetary policy.

He said corporate tax rates had earlier been expected to fall to 33 percent. The State Bank of Pakistan policy was likely to raise financing costs for capital-intensive industries. However, Style predicted an earnings growth of 22 percent in 1997/98, assuming improved economic and political conditions.
"We expect elections to take place as scheduled in February 1997, after which we expect to see a further consolidation of the reform process initiated by the caretaker administration."

He said Jardine Fleming saw good prospects for the power, fertiliser, synthetic fibre and telecommunication sectors. "We see room for strong growth in each of these sectors in terms of profits as well as share price performance," Style added.
He said progress on privatisation hinged on macro-economic stability, which has so far proved elusive.
Jardine Fleming was a global coordinator of Pakistan's largest foreign placement, $898 million of vouchers of state-run Pakistan Telecommunication Co Ltd in November 1994.
Plans to sell a 26 percent management stake in the telecom utility to a foreign investor have hit snags, but the government believes a deal can be cut in the next six to 12 months.

Style said it would be hard for the caretaker government to complete sales of large state-run corporations, but it should be able to appoint advisers, establish regulatory agencies and frameworks that could ease the task for an elected government.

He said Jardine Fleming's plan to get KSE membership through its Pakistani brokerage wing, Jardine Fleming Pakistan Broking (Private) Ltd, was part of a long-term strategy to offer clients a comprehensive service throughout its franchise area.
"If foreign investors perceive our aquisition of a seat on the KSE as a vote of confidence in the future of Pakistan, we are pleased to be seen as supportive of the local capital markets," he said.
The KSE has deferred Jardine Fleming's application for membership pending identification of a local partner as required for foreign brokerages to operate in the bourse.
